outcome: Since 26 January 2024 the problem has moved only through two unrefereed manuscripts released by OpenAI on 6 October 2026 that claim a negative answer (a finite lattice that is the congruence lattice of no finite algebra); no human-refereed resolution, and no published or independently verified one, exists as of 11 October 2026, and the group-theoretic step the negative answer rests on is reported as unchecked outside OpenAI.
problem_asks: (1) Whether every finite lattice L is isomorphic (as a lattice) to Con(A), the congruence lattice of some finite algebra A. (2) The quantifier 'some finite algebra' does not fix the signature or the number of operations; the question covers finite algebras with any finite signature. (3) The question is universal over all finite lattices and asks for a yes or no: a positive answer requires a representing finite algebra for every finite lattice, and a negative answer requires one finite lattice with no representing finite algebra. The statement gives no bound on the size of the lattice or of the algebra. Equivalently, by the Pálfy–Pudlák result of 1980, whether every finite lattice is an interval [D,G] in the subgroup lattice of some finite group; that equivalence is outside the statement itself but is the route the literature uses to reach it.

events.what_happened: P. P. Pálfy and P. Pudlák prove that 'every finite lattice is isomorphic to Con(A) for some finite algebra A' is equivalent to 'every finite lattice is isomorphic to an interval in the subgroup lattice of some finite group' (Algebra Universalis 11(1), 1980, pp. 22–27). This is a reduction, not a case of the problem. Cited in the Wikipedia article and in the OPG entry; the 1980 paper itself was not readable here (see incomplete).
events.delivers: The equivalence of the two universal statements: the congruence form of the problem holds exactly when the interval form holds. It establishes no particular lattice either way.
events.remains: The whole problem; the reduction changes which question is open, not whether it is open.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper after refereeing (inferred from publication; the referee process was not inspected)

events.direction: Neutral reduction; does not assert either answer.

events.what_happened: William J. DeMeo, 'Congruence lattices of finite algebras' (arXiv:1204.4305; PhD thesis, University of Hawaii, 114 pages). Using a new method together with known ones and computer software (UACalc and GAP), he shows that every lattice with at most seven elements is the congruence lattice of a finite algebra, with one possible exception, which he identifies as the smallest lattice with no known representation.
events.revisions: v1 19 Apr 2012; v2 21 Apr 2012; v3 7 May 2012 (current, per the arXiv listing).
events.delivers: Representations of all lattices with at most seven elements, with one exception. Restricted to lattices of size seven or less; says nothing about lattices with eight or more elements.
events.remains: All finite lattices with eight or more elements, and the one exceptional lattice of at most seven elements.

events.what_happened: Sebastien Palcoux and Pablo Spiga, 'Sharp bounds for intervals in finite subgroup lattices' (arXiv:2609.10343, math.GR, single version, submitted 9 Sep 2026). For H ≤ G with index n > 1 and p the least prime divisor of n, the number of subgroups K with H ≤ K ≤ G is bounded by c(p)·n^((log_p n)/4); the authors claim exponent and constant are optimal, already for elementary abelian p-groups of even rank. The acknowledgements state that the manuscript was prepared with assistance from two named models. Discarded for this problem: it bounds the size of subgroup intervals and does not address which finite lattices are intervals.
events.delivers: An upper bound on the size of a subgroup interval [H,G] as a function of its index n, sharp in exponent and constant. Restriction: an upper bound on interval size with the index free, so it constrains only small indices and excludes no particular finite lattice from being an interval.
events.remains: The whole problem: no finite lattice is shown to be or not to be an interval of a finite group's subgroup lattice.

events.what_happened: OpenAI released 'A negative solution to the finite lattice representation problem' in the openai/math repository on 6 Oct 2026, as part of a batch of 722 manuscripts (719 after withdrawals) from an unreleased internal model. The paper (listed as a preprint, author line 'OpenAI', no human named) is labelled with a folder date of 24 September 2026, but I found no public posting before the 6 October release. Its abstract reads: 'We give a negative solution to the finite lattice representation problem.' Its introduction states the two main results: (congruence form) there exists a finite nonempty lattice that is not the full congruence lattice of any finite nonempty algebra of any finite signature; (subgroup form) there is a finite lattice, self-dual, not isomorphic to [D,G] for any subgroup D of any finite group G. The paper says the subgroup form implies the congruence form by a global transfer (via Pálfy–Pudlák). Per DeMeo's review (7 Oct 2026) the paper runs to 87 pages and its weight rests on a chain-rigidity theorem with an absolute but uncomputed constant B. Family 206 in the repository's CONTENTS.md is titled 'Finite lattice representation and undecidability' and lists this paper together with its companion.
events.revisions: Released 6 Oct 2026. The repository change log (history.md) has one entry, dated 7 Oct 2026, withdrawing three other manuscripts (Hodge-related) and revising fourteen; none of the revised groups is this paper. No later revision found in what I could read. The folder label 'September 24, 2026' is the manuscript's date, not a posting date.
events.delivers: Asserts a negative answer: a specific finite nonempty lattice (a member L_N of an explicit family, for N at least max{2, ⌈B⌉}, where B is an absolute constant asserted to exist by contradiction and never computed) that is not isomorphic to Con(A) for any finite nonempty algebra A of any finite signature. Route: a self-dual finite lattice that is not a subgroup interval of any finite group (main:group), transferred to algebras by Pálfy–Pudlák. Restrictions: the existence of L_N depends on the chain-rigidity theorem (the absolute constant B, proved by contradiction using the classification of finite simple groups, finite Ramsey theory and cited results), which is the step the paper's own text presents as proved in a section I could read only in part.
events.remains: If the argument is correct, nothing of the problem as stated remains open: a counterexample is claimed. Still unestablished in the record: the chain-rigidity theorem and the Propositions it relies on in other sections (cls:reduction, grw:remaining-paths, lift:edge-lifts, pkt:bounded-length), which I did not read in full.

checked_by.qualification: Author of the 2012 thesis and arXiv paper on this problem (event demeo-2012-small-lattices) and of the Open Problem Garden entry for it; a working expert in congruence lattices of finite algebras.
checked_by.what_they_did: Wrote a blog review on 7 Oct 2026 after reading the manuscripts. Reports that Claude checked Sections 2, 8, 9 and 10 of the main paper line by line, that these checks are the model's and not a referee's, and that 'as far as I know no one outside OpenAI has yet checked the group theory of Sections 3 to 7'. Calls the negative answer 'plausible and not yet refereed' and says he would not cite it as established yet. Reports that the lattice-theoretic half holds up in the AI-assisted reading and that the weight rests on the unverified chain theorem.

events.directly_checkable: The lattice family L_N = B_N ⊞ B_N^op ⊞ E_N ⊞ E_N^op (horizontal sum of decorated components, each of size at most 9(q_0 + 27hN^2)) is explicit once B is known. B is not computed, so no particular member can be checked by hand from the record.
events.doubts: (1) Chain rigidity (absolute B) is the load-bearing group-theoretic step. DeMeo reports it unchecked outside OpenAI for Sections 3–7. It is proved by contradiction using classification-of-finite-simple-groups inputs (Proposition 2.3 cites them), finite Ramsey theory, and cited results (Burness–Testerman, Conrad, Dowd–Sin, Steinberg, Burness–Liebeck–Shalev, Aschbacher and others). (2) B is only shown to exist; no member of the family is named explicitly, and the lattices section does not state outright that a member is not a subgroup interval (my reading: the proof derives label equalities forced in any subgroup-interval representation, which would have to be checked). (3) The lattice half was checked line by line by a model (Claude), not by a referee. (4) The main theorem is not formalised (DeMeo); the formal material is partial. (5) The same batch contains three manuscripts withdrawn for a sign error and fourteen revised; none is this paper, but the process has produced errors elsewhere. (6) The repository states that results are at different verification stages and that 'some of the unformalized results could have issues'. Prompts were not released; the one-prompt, single-agent account is reported by a secondary outlet and is disputed as unverified by MIT's Andrew Sutherland. Context, not a doubt: many experts expected a negative answer (OPG conjecture; a 2020 survey).
events.direction: Negative: claims that the problem's answer is no, i.e., some finite lattice is not Con(A) for any finite algebra. Consistent with the Open Problem Garden conjecture and the view many experts reportedly hold.
events.object: A finite nonempty lattice L_N for N = max{2, ⌈B⌉}, built as the horizontal sum B_N ⊞ B_N^op ⊞ E_N ⊞ E_N^op of a decorated Boolean component and a decorated detector component (each of size at most 9(q_0 + 27hN²)). It is claimed to be non-representable because the chain-rigidity theorem forces label equalities in any subgroup-interval representation. The constant B is non-constructive: proved to exist by contradiction, never computed, so the specific member is not identified. Also the subgroup-form object: a finite self-dual lattice that is not a subgroup interval of any finite group, derived from the same family, with the same non-constructive threshold.

events.what_happened: OpenAI released the companion 'Finite congruence lattices: characterization and undecidability' in the same repository on 6 Oct 2026 (folder label 24 Sep 2026; author line 'OpenAI'; no human named). Its abstract: an explicit colored-graph characterization of the finite nonempty lattices that are full congruence lattices of finite algebras; undecidability of deciding this representation property; 'In particular, the finite lattice representation problem has a negative answer'; and undecidability of recognising full subgroup intervals in finite groups. Its introduction's main theorem: (i) representable iff satisfies the finite colored-graph criterion; (ii) no Turing machine decides representability from the order table of a finite nonempty lattice; (iii) there is a nonrepresentable finite lattice L_0 of minimum cardinality, specified by finite formulas (through a Busy Beaver constant), with every smaller lattice representable and |L_0| > 7; (iv) it is undecidable whether L ≅ [H,G] for some finite group G and subgroup H.
events.revisions: Released 6 Oct 2026. Not named in the 7 Oct 2026 change log entry. No later revision found in what I could read.
events.delivers: A colored-graph criterion for representability (a finite test for each graph size, not a decision procedure); undecidability of representability from an order table; a specified minimum nonrepresentable lattice with cardinality above seven, not evaluated; undecidability of subgroup-interval recognition. The abstract says the problem has a negative answer. Logic I checked: undecidability of a property over all finite lattices implies some lattice lacks it, since a property held by every lattice would be trivially decidable; so the negative answer follows from the undecidability claim if that claim holds. Restriction: the derivation depends on the undecidability sections, which I did not read.
events.remains: If the undecidability and minimum-lattice claims hold, the problem is answered negatively as stated. Not verified in the record: the undecidability argument (sections 5–14 and 16 per DeMeo, which he did not read), and the minimum-lattice specification, which is not evaluated.

Says sections 5–14 and 16, which carry the undecidability weight, were not read. Describes the minimum-lattice argument as logically sound but giving no way to find or compute the lattice.

events.directly_checkable: The colored-graph criterion can be checked on small lattices. The minimum lattice L_0 is not evaluated, so no particular non-representable lattice is checkable from the record.
events.doubts: (1) The undecidability argument (Theorem 15.3 and Corollary 15.4 in the companion's numbering) lies in sections I did not read and that DeMeo did not read. (2) The paper's own text says a decider exists if and only if a computable bound on witness sizes exists, and its argument for undecidability rests on showing no such bound exists; that step is unchecked here. (3) The minimum lattice is specified but its cardinality and order table are not evaluated; the Busy Beaver constant is not computed. (4) Formal coverage is the colored-graph criterion only (see machine_checked). (5) Its negative answer is a corollary of its undecidability claim, so it stands or falls with (1) and (2). (6) It has no acknowledgement or AI-use statement in the parts I read.
events.direction: Negative answer (per its abstract), delivered via undecidability and a minimum counterexample; also a characterization.
events.object: (a) The colored-graph criterion: a finite nonempty lattice is representable exactly when it has a finite nonempty lattice-colored graph witness; a finite test per graph size, not a decision procedure. (b) A minimum nonrepresentable finite lattice L_0 with |L_0| > 7, specified by finite formulas in the paper's minimum section and tied to a Busy Beaver constant; cardinality and order table not evaluated; non-constructive in that its size is not computed. (c) The undecidability claims themselves are results about decision procedures, not lattices.

summary: The problem has moved only through OpenAI's release of 6 October 2026, and no independent, refereed check exists yet. The openai/math repository holds two manuscripts in family 206 ('Finite lattice representation and undecidability'), both folder-dated 24 September 2026 but first publicly posted on the 6 October release, as far as I could find. The first, 'A negative solution to the finite lattice representation problem', claims a finite lattice that is the congruence lattice of no finite algebra, via a self-dual finite lattice that is no subgroup interval of a finite group and the Pálfy–Pudlák transfer; its weight rests on a chain-rigidity theorem with an absolute constant B that is proved to exist by contradiction, using classification of finite simple groups and cited results, and never computed. The companion, 'Finite congruence lattices: characterization and undecidability', gives a colored-graph criterion, claims undecidability of representability and of subgroup-interval recognition, specifies a minimum nonrepresentable lattice of size above seven without evaluating it, and states in its abstract that the problem 'has a negative answer'. The only independent engagement I found is William DeMeo's blog review of 7 October 2026, from a qualified author on this problem: he reports that Claude checked Sections 2, 8, 9 and 10 of the main paper line by line, that this is not a referee's verification, that as far as he knows no one outside OpenAI has checked the group theory of Sections 3–7, and that the undecidability claim is more exposed than the negative answer. He calls the negative answer 'plausible and not yet refereed'. The release states that the vast majority of results came from an unreleased internal OpenAI model; the manuscripts name no human, and the build sources of the main paper carry no acknowledgement or AI-use statement. Formal status is partial: the comparator challenge stub for the colored-graph criterion contains one sorry and its solution module contains none by textual reading (I did not compile it); the main theorem of the first paper is not formalised, and the formalization catalogue has no entry for either paper. The batch's three withdrawals (7 Oct, sign error) and fourteen revisions name other topics, not this one. Two readings are close. Read as a resolution: the claim is explicit in structure, and a non-constructive B suffices for an existence claim, so if the chain theorem holds the problem is answered negatively as stated, with the lattice half reported as checked (by a model). Read as unsettled: the decisive step is an unrefereed group-theoretic theorem that, on the record, no specialist outside the company has examined, and the Lean material does not cover the negative answer. Separately, Palcoux and Spiga (arXiv:2609.10343, 9 Sep 2026) prove sharp size bounds for subgroup intervals and acknowledge assistance from GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-6 Astra; it bears on intervals in sizes only, excludes no lattice, and is recorded as discarded. Pre-window results are the 1980 Pálfy–Pudlák reduction and DeMeo's 2012 representation of all lattices up to seven elements with one exception; nothing before 2026 is a resolution. Searches for responses from Pálfy, Kearnes, Freese, Jipsen, Nation, MathOverflow and arXiv turned up none on this claim as of 11 October 2026. I did not verify the OpenAI announcement page itself (403), and the manuscript text I read came through a fetch tool that returns model-rendered output, so the quotations should be spot-checked against the PDF or TeX source.
competing_reading: For counting it as a resolution: the claim is a complete negative answer as stated, and existence of a counterexample needs no computed constant, so the uncomputed B is no obstacle to settling the question. The lattice half is reported as checked line by line; the undecidability companion is not needed for the negative answer, which is supported by the first paper alone. Being unrefereed is the normal state of a 2026 preprint, and the repository is a public, versioned release with a documented change log. Against it: the entire negative answer depends on an unrefereed chain theorem that the record shows was read by the company's model and one blogger only in part; the group-theoretic inputs are many and cited rather than verified; the Lean does not cover the negative answer; and the same batch has already produced sign-error withdrawals. The problem as the literature understands it is open until specialists accept the group theory.
what_would_settle_it: A referee report or publication of 'A negative solution to the finite lattice representation problem', or an independent specialist account of Sections 3–7 and the chain-rigidity theorem with its classification inputs; a compiled, sorry-free Lean proof of the congruence theorem (or of the subgroup theorem plus the Pálfy–Pudlák transfer) with its axioms checked; a compiled check of the GraphCriterion solution against its challenge; an explicit computed value of B, or an explicit small lattice certified non-representable; or a published error in the chain-rigidity step.
